title: 05 — Credit Risk Modelling
html:
05 — Credit Risk Modelling

The one idea: a credit model estimates the probability that a borrower defaults over a horizon. It must rank borrowers well, give calibrated probabilities, behave in ways a credit committee can explain, and be governed like any model that moves money.

1. What it is

Term Meaning
PD Probability of default over a horizon, usually 12 months
LGD Loss given default: the share of exposure lost if default happens
EAD Exposure at default
Expected loss PD × LGD × EAD. The building block of provisioning (such as expected credit loss)
Scorecard A points-based model, usually WoE-encoded logistic regression
WoE Weight of evidence per bin: ln(share of goods / share of bads)
IV Information value: how strongly a binned feature separates goods from bads
Gini, KS Discrimination measures: Gini = 2 × AUC − 1, and KS = the largest gap between the cumulative good and bad distributions
Rating transition matrix Probability of moving from each rating grade to each other grade over a period

2. Why it matters

  • Early-warning signals, issuer risk scores and credit products are PD models in practice.
  • Regulators and model-risk teams expect explainability, stability and documentation, which shapes the method as much as accuracy does.
  • The data platform supplies the inputs (financials, pledges, ratings, defaults), so the engineer must know what "default" and "as of" mean.

3. The main ideas, beginner to expert

3.1 Beginner: define the target carefully

  • Default definition: for example, 90 or more days past due, a D rating, or a distressed restructuring. Write it down and version it.
  • Observation date and horizon: "as of 31 March, did default happen within 12 months?". Features must be point-in-time as of the observation date (02).
  • Exclusions: entities already in default, or too young to observe a full horizon.

3.2 Intermediate: the scorecard workflow

---
title: Scorecard development workflow
---
flowchart LR
    T["Target and sample<br/>(definition, horizon, exclusions)"] --> B["Bin each feature<br/>(monotone bad rate)"]
    B --> W["WoE per bin, IV per feature<br/>drop weak or unstable features"]
    W --> LR["Logistic regression<br/>on WoE values"]
    LR --> S["Scale to points<br/>(offset, factor)"]
    S --> V["Validate: Gini, KS, calibration,<br/>stability (PSI), out-of-time sample"]
    V --> G["Document, approve, monitor"]

Rules of thumb often quoted for IV: under 0.02 not useful, 0.02 to 0.1 weak, 0.1 to 0.3 medium, above 0.3 strong. These are conventions, so check them against your own data. Very high IV can signal leakage.

Points scaling: points = offset + factor × ln(odds of good), with factor = PDO / ln 2 (PDO means points to double the odds).

3.3 Senior: calibration, stability and governance

  • Calibrate to a long-run default rate, not one benign year. Check predicted against observed per score band.
  • Out-of-time validation: test on a later period, not just a random holdout.
  • Stability: monitor the score distribution (PSI, see drift statistics) and feature drift.
  • Model risk governance: an inventory, independent validation, documented assumptions and limits, approvals, periodic review, and challenger models. Check your regulator's current model-risk expectations with your risk team.
  • Fairness and explainability: reason codes (the top factors lowering a score) for every decision.

4. Working code

The script builds a made-up loan book (3.2% defaults), bins two features, computes WoE and IV, fits a WoE-encoded logistic regression, scales it to scorecard points (600 points at 50:1 odds, 20 points to double the odds), and reports AUC, Gini and KS. numpy and pandas.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
# Made-up loan book: interest coverage and promoter pledge drive default within 12 months.
n = 6000
coverage = np.clip(rng.lognormal(1.2, 0.6, n), 0.2, 20)
pledge = np.clip(rng.beta(1.2, 4, n) * 100, 0, 100)                       # % of promoter shares pledged
logit = -3.4 - 0.45 * np.log(coverage) * 2 + 0.03 * pledge
default = (rng.random(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)
df = pd.DataFrame({"coverage": coverage, "pledge": pledge, "default": default})
print(f"default rate: {df.default.mean():.3%}")

# 1. Weight of evidence (WoE) and information value (IV) per binned feature.
def woe_table(df, col, bins):
    g = df.groupby(pd.cut(df[col], bins), observed=True)["default"].agg(["count", "sum"])
    g["good"], g["bad"] = g["count"] - g["sum"], g["sum"]
    dist_good, dist_bad = g["good"] / g["good"].sum(), g["bad"] / g["bad"].sum()
    g["woe"] = np.log(dist_good / dist_bad)
    g["iv_part"] = (dist_good - dist_bad) * g["woe"]
    return g[["count", "bad", "woe", "iv_part"]]
cov_t = woe_table(df, "coverage", [0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 21])
pl_t = woe_table(df, "pledge", [-0.1, 5, 20, 40, 101])
print(cov_t.round(3).to_string()); print("IV coverage:", round(cov_t.iv_part.sum(), 3))
print(pl_t.round(3).to_string()); print("IV pledge:", round(pl_t.iv_part.sum(), 3))

# 2. Scorecard: WoE-encoded logistic regression, then points = offset - factor * log-odds.
def woe_encode(s, table, bins):
    return pd.cut(s, bins).map(table["woe"]).astype(float).to_numpy()
X = np.column_stack([woe_encode(df.coverage, cov_t, [0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 21]),
                     woe_encode(df.pledge, pl_t, [-0.1, 5, 20, 40, 101])])
w, b = np.zeros(2), 0.0
for _ in range(3000):                                                    # plain gradient descent
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ w + b)))
    w -= 0.5 * X.T @ (p - default) / n; b -= 0.5 * (p - default).mean()
p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ w + b)))
factor = 20 / np.log(2)                     # 20 points to double the odds of being good
offset = 600 - factor * np.log(50)          # 600 points at good:bad odds of 50:1
score = offset + factor * np.log((1 - p) / p)
print(f"score range {score.min():.0f} to {score.max():.0f}; mean score of defaulters "
      f"{score[default == 1].mean():.0f} vs non-defaulters {score[default == 0].mean():.0f}")

# 3. Discrimination: Gini = 2*AUC - 1, and KS = max gap between the cumulative good and bad distributions.
order = np.argsort(p)
ranks = np.empty(n); ranks[order] = np.arange(1, n + 1)
pos = default == 1
auc = (ranks[pos].sum() - pos.sum() * (pos.sum() + 1) / 2) / (pos.sum() * (~pos).sum())
s_sorted = np.sort(score)
cum_bad = np.searchsorted(np.sort(score[pos]), s_sorted, side="right") / pos.sum()
cum_good = np.searchsorted(np.sort(score[~pos]), s_sorted, side="right") / (~pos).sum()
print(f"AUC {auc:.3f}  Gini {2 * auc - 1:.3f}  KS {np.max(cum_bad - cum_good):.3f}")

Output:

default rate: 3.200%
          count  bad    woe  iv_part
coverage                            
(0, 1]      140   12 -1.042    0.042
(1, 2]     1026   59 -0.613    0.086
(2, 4]     2528   86 -0.063    0.002
(4, 8]     1860   30  0.701    0.111
(8, 21]     446    5  1.070    0.053
IV coverage: 0.295
               count  bad    woe  iv_part
pledge                                   
(-0.1, 5.0]      771   13  0.656    0.041
(5.0, 20.0]     2354   47  0.484    0.074
(20.0, 40.0]    1870   71 -0.177    0.011
(40.0, 101.0]   1005   61 -0.670    0.104
IV pledge: 0.23
score range 535 to 637; mean score of defaulters 578 vs non-defaulters 593
AUC 0.691  Gini 0.382  KS 0.294

What to notice:

  • WoE moves monotonically for both features: higher coverage is safer and higher pledge is riskier. That is what a credit committee expects to see.
  • IV of 0.295 (coverage) and 0.23 (pledge) count as "medium" by the usual convention. Both are useful, and neither is suspiciously high.
  • Gini 0.382 and KS 0.294 are typical of a two-feature model. Real scorecards add more features, but must stay explainable.

5. Common mistakes

  1. A vague default definition. The model learns whatever the label happens to be.
  2. Features not as of the observation date. Leakage from later financials or rating actions.
  3. Non-monotone bins. Hard to explain, and often noise. Merge bins until the bad rate is monotone.
  4. Calibrating on one benign year. PDs are then too low for the cycle.
  5. No monitoring. Population shifts silently degrade the model.

6. Exercise (2 hours)

  1. Add a third feature (rating notches lost in 12 months), bin it, and check its IV.
  2. Produce reason codes: for each borrower, the feature whose bin costs the most points relative to the best bin.
  3. Split the made-up book into two "years" with different default rates, and test calibration out of time.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What is the formula for expected loss?
  2. What does a negative WoE mean for a bin?
  3. How are Gini and AUC related?
  4. Why validate out of time?
  5. What does PDO mean in scorecard scaling?

Answers

  1. PD × LGD × EAD.
  2. The bin's share of bads is larger than its share of goods, so it is riskier than average.
  3. Gini = 2 × AUC − 1.
  4. Because the model will be used on future periods, and relationships drift over time.
  5. Points to double the odds: how many score points correspond to doubling the good-to-bad odds.

8. Sources

Checked 2026-10-26. The examples are original. For background:

  • Siddiqi, Credit Risk Scorecards (Wiley), the standard practitioner text on WoE and IV.
  • Basel Committee, IRB approach overview: https://www.bis.org/basel_framework/
